newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Traders cut Argentine wheat sowing forecasts.
newsitem.headline: Traders cut Argentine wheat sowing forecasts.

text.p: Argentine farmers will only sow 5.5-6.0 million hectares with 1997/98 wheat, a big fall both from last season's 7.3 million hectares and from early season expectations, traders said Wednesday.
"Many in the trade are at 5.5 million hectares, and everyone's under six million hectares," a trader told Reuters.
Another agreed: "I am estimating 20-25 percent less area than last year, which gives 5.6-5.9 million hectares."
Such an area would yield a bit more than 12.5 million tonnes, given normal weather from now on, he said.
The government's Agricultural Secretariat last Wednesday said that it had cut its estimate of wheat area to 6.25 million hectares from 6.5 million hectares.

Heavy autumn and early winter rain in much of the grain belt, particarly in the lush wheat heartlands of southern Buenos Aires province, combined with lingering drought in the less important areas of Cordoba and Santa Fe to delay early sowing of longer-cycle varieties, traders said.

Delays led some farmers already tempted by good soy prices to drop wheat for first crop soybeans in places like northern Buenos Aires. One trader said that he thought 3.0-3.3 million hectares had been sown to date.

In parts of the important southern end of the wheat belt, sowing is only 10-15 percent complete, a trader said, and more rain could mean more delays. But he pointed out that southern planting can continue as late as September if necessary.
But the wheat which has been sown has flourished due to the generous soil moisture levels, traders said.
"It's in great shape everywhere. Soil moisture is very good," one said.

Traders said the southern oscillation index was providing clear evidence that the the El Nino weather event is taking effect, which should mean continuing wet weather throughout the Argentine grain belt at least for the rest of the winter.
"The rain should not be too much of a problem for yields. The alarm bells for yields are sounding because fertilizer sales are down," a trader said.
He said that accumulated sales were 50 percent below what had been sold by the same date last season.
But another trader played down the fertilizer fears.
"I hear they're selling less too, but only 20 percent or so less," he said, "And in many areas you hear that the farmers are using it more efficiently this year."
Fertilizer use boomed last season as decades of under-investment in Argentine farming began to be reversed.
